newsitem.title: USA: U.S. prosecutors call defense tactic pulp fiction.
newsitem.headline: U.S. prosecutors call defense tactic pulp fiction.

text.p: Prosecutors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Thursday told a federal appeals court a defence request for information from government intelligence agencies "reads like a bad Hollywood script."
The government lawyers told the court that defence suggestions that international terrorists were behind the bombing "is not a serious pleading" and is "patently frivolous."

On Tuesday lawyers for bombing defendant Timothy McVeigh asked the federal appeals court to delay the March 31 start of his trial until the court decides if prosecutors must provide the defence with classified intelligence data from the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Security Agency among others.

The defence team said it needed the material to investigate its theory that a foreign government, possibly Iraq, may have planned the bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, which killed 168 people.
Prosecutors in their filing with the appeals court said they saw no reason to respond further because Tuesday's request "is a bad work of fiction."

"We are prepared to rebut McVeigh's pulp fiction with provable facts -- to prove that there was no international terrorist coalition behind the murder in Oklahoma City, no prior warning and no mastermind other than McVeigh and his co-defendant," lead prosecutor Joseph Hartzler wrote in a three-paragraph filing.
The prosecution accused McVeigh's attorneys of seeking the intelligence information to evade the trial judge's prohibition on public comment by the attorneys.
Last Friday U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch issued an absolute gag order at least until a jury is seated. The trial is scheduled to begin on Monday with jury selection.
The prosecutors claimed that McVeigh's attorneys were merely trying to publicise "many of the spurious claims the trial judge sealed (and rejected as insupportable)."
On Wednesday McVeigh's lawyers asked the appeals court to delay the trial until they can challenge a law that allows victims to both view the trial and testify too.
McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols are charged in the bombing and, if convicted, face the death penalty. Nichols will be tried separately at an undetermined date.
